name: Real World Data Deals
blurb: Drugmakers buying AI ready clinical and molecular data.
title: Real World Data Deals
answer: Precision medicine data companies license multimodal clinical and genomic data to drugmakers for AI driven research and evidence. Tempus signed strategic collaborations with Merck and with Gilead giving enterprise access to its data platform and analytical services.

reading.body:
Licensed real world data reaches AI drug research through multiyear collaborations, not open datasets, and the licence terms decide what the models may learn.

The pattern is a small number of precision medicine data companies holding linked clinical, genomic, imaging and outcomes data, mostly oncology, and licensing enterprise access plus analytical services to drugmakers. Tempus signed strategic collaborations with Merck and with Gilead in 2026, one aimed at AI driven precision medicine and one at oncology research through real world evidence. Oncology data is valuable because cancer treatment depends heavily on molecular profiling, so linked clinical and genomic records are unusually informative for finding biomarkers, designing trials and identifying patients.

For AI specifically, this is a data supply chain rather than a compute story. The constraint is not chips or power but consent, de-identification and contract language: whether licensed patient data may train models at all, who owns the models and insights built on it, and how long access lasts. A commercial team's first check is the consent and de-identification terms in the licence, before any training use.

What this does not cover is scale. There are no contract values, no data volumes, no patient counts and no model performance figures here, so the size of these deals and their effect on research output cannot be judged from this data. It also names only one company, so it shows a deal shape rather than the breadth of the market.

explainer:
Precision medicine data companies collect large, linked datasets: clinical records, genomic sequencing, imaging and outcomes, often from oncology. Drugmakers license access to these data to find biomarkers, design trials, identify patients and generate real world evidence, and increasingly to train AI models.

Deals are usually multiyear subscriptions or strategic collaborations covering data access and analytical services. The important details sit in the terms: how the data were consented and de-identified, whether they may be used to train models, who owns models and insights built on them, and how long access lasts.

What is being bought

Real world data means records generated outside clinical trials: insurance claims, electronic health records, pharmacy fills, registries, wearables and increasingly genomic data linked to medical histories. Deals range from a licence to query a de-identified database, to multi year partnerships in which a data company builds custom cohorts and analytics for one drug maker, to outright acquisitions of data businesses. AI has raised the price because models trained on large linked patient histories can now support uses that older statistical methods could not, such as finding patients for trials or predicting which patients will respond.

Why the deals are growing

Regulators now accept real world evidence for some decisions, especially label expansions, post approval safety commitments and rare disease studies where trials are impractical. Commercial teams want the same data to understand treatment patterns and to target outreach. Both uses depend on data that is linked across sources and refreshed often, which is expensive to assemble and therefore worth paying a specialist for.

The cautions

Privacy law differs by country and is changing, de-identification can fail when datasets are linked, and consent given for care does not always cover commercial analysis. Regulators also scrutinise whether a dataset is fit for the question asked: a claims database that misses over the counter medicines or lab values can mislead. Good contracts cover provenance, permitted uses, re-identification safeguards and what happens to derived models if the deal ends.
